actions.target: Aditya's launch announcement for How to Build an Agentic CRM: A Reference Architecture
actions.text: To turn the architecture into an acceptance test, I would inject two copies of the same CRM event and then drop the response after the first committed write. The retry should resolve the recorded outcome, not create a second business effect; a changed record version should return for reassessment. I would measure duplicate effects per 1,000 attempted actions and the age of unresolved outcomes separately from API success rate. That test would come before any expansion of the agent's write scope.

actions.target: Karthikeyan Palanisamy's KCS and shared-business-vocabulary article; top-level comment
actions.text: Karthikeyan Palanisamy, reuse is evidence that a term is useful, but its frequency alone cannot authorize a business definition. I would promote a KCS-discovered term into the semantic layer with a named owner, an effective version and executable examples: for 'active customer', include one record Sales includes and Finance excludes, then expose the chosen definition. Track disagreement rate on an adjudicated test set and downstream decisions affected by a definition change. How do you resolve competing definitions before agents can act on them?

actions.target: Aditya Singh's personal LinkedIn feed; a resurfacing post for Read. Reflect. Rise., not a new newsletter edition
actions.text:
Five working days of release waiting can consume 26.7 hours of rework in a simple CRM routing scenario.

The example in my Read. Reflect. Rise. edition assumes 400 records a day, a 4% misrouting rate and 20 minutes to repair each exception:
400 × 0.04 × 20 ÷ 60 = 5.33 rework hours per day.
Five days at that rate = 26.7 hours.

This is modeled workload, not a measured customer result. It excludes lost opportunities and customer impact.

The useful management question is which change deserves a faster, controlled path. For a reversible routing rule, I would require a named policy owner, an approved version and a tested recovery route. Then track waiting time alongside bad changes and recovery time; a shorter queue is not a win if mistakes become harder to contain.

The full edition explains the policy and execution split:
https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/3-minute-decision-took-3-weeks-ship-aditya-singh-kmejc/
